content: CD135, also referred to as FLT3 (Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3), is a receptor-type tyrosine-protein kinase encoded by the FLT3 gene in humans. It functions as a cytokine receptor and is classified as a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase class III family. CD135 serves as the receptor for the cytokine FLT3 ligand (FLT3L) and is predominantly expressed on the surface of various hematopoietic progenitor cells. The signaling pathway mediated by FLT3 is critical for the normal development of hematopoietic stem cells and progenitor cells. Mutations in the FLT3 gene are among the most frequently observed genetic alterations in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Even in AML patients without FLT3 mutations, elevated levels of wild-type FLT3 have been detected in blast cells, and these high levels are often associated with a poorer prognosis. Structurally, FLT3 consists of five extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, an extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, a juxtamembrane domain, and a tyrosine kinase domain composed of two lobes connected by a tyrosine kinase insert. The cytoplasmic form of FLT3 undergoes glycosylation, which facilitates its localization to the cell membrane. Functionally, CD135 is a class III receptor tyrosine kinase. Upon binding to FLT3L, a ternary complex is formed, where two FLT3 molecules are bridged by a single homodimeric FLT3L. This complex formation brings the intracellular domains of the two FLT3 molecules into close proximity, initiating trans-phosphorylation of the kinase domains. This phosphorylation event activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, which subsequently phosphorylates and activates downstream signal transduction molecules, propagating the signal within the cell. CD135 signaling plays a pivotal role in cell survival, proliferation, and differentiation. It is essential for the development of lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) but is not required for the development of other blood cell lineages, such as myeloid cells. Two cytokines, TNF-alpha (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) and TGF-beta (transforming growth factor-beta), downregulate FLT3 activity. TGF-beta, in particular, reduces FLT3 protein levels and reverses the FLT3L-induced shortening of the G1 phase in the cell cycle of hematopoietic progenitors. Clinically, CD135 is an important cell surface marker used to identify specific types of hematopoietic progenitors in the bone marrow. Multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) express high levels of CD135 on their surface. This marker is used to distinguish hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which are CD135-negative, from MPPs, which are CD135-positive. CD135 is also a proto-oncogene, meaning that mutations in this protein can lead to cancer. Mutations in the FLT3 receptor are implicated in the development of leukemia, particularly acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a malignancy of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors. Internal tandem duplications (ITDs) of FLT3 (FLT3-ITD) are the most common mutations associated with AML and are considered a prognostic indicator linked to adverse disease outcomes. FLT3 inhibitors are being actively developed and tested for therapeutic use in AML. Gilteritinib, a dual FLT3-AXL tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is undergoing multiple Phase III clinical trials for AML and received FDA orphan drug status in 2017. Quizartinib (AC220) demonstrated promising results in a Phase II clinical trial for AML patients with FLT3 mutations, particularly in refractory AML patients who subsequently underwent stem cell transplantation. Midostaurin was approved by the FDA in April 2017 for the treatment of adult patients with newly diagnosed AML harboring oncogenic FLT3 mutations, in combination with chemotherapy. This approval includes the use of a companion diagnostic, the LeukoStrat CDx FLT3 Mutation Assay, to detect FLT3 mutations in AML patients. Sorafenib has shown significant activity against FLT3-ITD-positive AML, and sunitinib also inhibits FLT3. Lestaurtinib is currently in clinical trials. A study published in Nature in April 2012 investigated patients who developed resistance to FLT3 inhibitors. The study identified specific DNA sites contributing to resistance and highlighted opportunities for the development of next-generation inhibitors that account for resistance-conferring mutations, aiming for more effective treatments.
